Wesel
vay'zel
n. (Lower Rhine city in the duchy of Cleves; refuge of the Dutch and Walloon exiles, and seat of the convent of 1568)
German Wesel, from a root meaning a wet meadow or the confluence, the town standing where the Lippe enters the Rhine.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Wesel was a Hanseatic city of the lower Rhine in the duchy of Cleves, and in the middle of the sixteenth century it became the chief landward refuge of the persecuted Reformed of the Netherlands and of the English Marian exiles. Its magistrates let the strangers in, let them worship, and let them organise, and the town earned in the exile literature the name of a hospitable city. From that crowded refugee community came the assembly which matters most. In November 1568, with the Duke of Alva in control of the Netherlands and the Reformed churches there driven underground or abroad, a gathering of ministers and elders at Wesel drew up a body of articles for the ordering of the Dutch Reformed churches—the offices of minister, elder and deacon, the examination and calling of ministers, the keeping of registers, the use of the Heidelberg Catechism and the Belgic Confession, the holding of classes and synods. It was not a lawful synod and it claimed nothing; it was a set of proposals by exiles for a church that did not yet legally exist, and it became the foundation of the church order which the synods of Emden and Dordrecht afterwards completed. The dictionary enters Wesel because a church order was drafted here by men with no buildings, no legal standing and no country, for congregations that were meeting in barns.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a refuge as shelter or protection from danger; hospitable as kind to strangers and guests; and a convent as an assembly of persons devoted to religion.

expand to see more

REFUGE, n. [L. refugium.] Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.

HOSPITABLE, adj. [L. hospitalis.] Receiving and entertaining strangers with kindness and without reward; kind to strangers and guests.

CONVENT, n. [L. conventus.] An assembly of persons devoted to religion; a body of monks or nuns; the house occupied by such a body.

ORDER, n. Regular disposition; established method; the system by which a church is governed; rule.

STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown; a guest.

Key Scripture

Heb 13:14 — "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Act 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

Modern Corruption

Lower Rhine refuge of the Dutch and English exiles, where the convent of 1568 drafted the church order of a church that did not yet legally exist.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of church order as a secondary matter, a question of administration to be settled by whatever works. The Wesel articles are the refutation. Men who had lost their houses and their country, who could offer their ministers no salary and their congregations no building, sat down in a refugee town and settled first the offices Christ gave the church, the manner of calling them, and the assemblies by which congregations help one another. They judged that a church without order is not persecuted but dissolved.

The principle to recover is that order is drawn from Scripture rather than from circumstance. “ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee” (Tit 1:5) was obeyed at Wesel in a form that the dictionary, holding congregational government with a plurality of elders, follows in substance though not in every particular. The articles were proposals, acknowledged as such, and were submitted to the churches: a model of how men should legislate for a church they do not own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner, a resident alien; Greek presbuteros (G4245), an elder.

expand to see more

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain, to continue; “here have we no continuing city”, Hebrews 13:14.

Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a sojourner in a strange place; “as strangers and pilgrims”, 1 Peter 2:11.

Greek presbuteros (G4245) — an elder, a church officer; “ordain elders in every city”, Titus 1:5.

Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to set in order, to appoint; “set in order the things that are wanting”, Titus 1:5.

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint by a show of hands; “when they had ordained them elders in every church”, Acts 14:23.

Usage

"“For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — the hospitable city of the Dutch and Walloon exiles."

"“ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee” (Tit 1:5) — the articles of November 1568."

"“when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) — a church order drafted for congregations meeting in barns."
